name: 203 Metre Hill
name_zh: 203高地 (203 Gāodì); Japanese monument: 尔灵山 (Ěrlíngshān)
name_now: The 203 memorial area on the fortress’s western front, with a cherry garden at its foot
summary: 203 Metre Hill stood outside the main ring of permanent forts and received no permanent fortifications under Velichko’s plan. After several days of fighting, Japanese troops took the summit on 5 December 1904 (22 November Old Style). It overlooked the inner basins, allowing observers to direct siege artillery onto ships at their moorings. The Japanese monument called Erlingshan stands on the summit. Sections of trenches survive, and the place where General Nogi’s son died is marked.
visit: There is parking at the entrance (203景区停车场). Admission is paid; check prices and hours locally. Travel agencies quoted 30 yuan in 2025. Prices may differ during the spring cherry-blossom season.

name: Fort No. II (North Fort of East Jiguan Shan)
name_zh: 东鸡冠山北堡垒 (Dōng Jīguānshān běi bǎolěi)
name_now: Dongjiguanshan visitor area, with the fort ruins and the Lüshun Russo-Japanese War Exhibition Hall (旅顺日俄战争陈列馆)
summary: A strongpoint on the northeastern front, where fighting for the counterscarp gallery continued for weeks, including underground. On 2 (15) December 1904, an 11-inch howitzer shell struck the officers’ casemate where General Roman Kondratenko was present; eight officers died with him. Three days later, on 18 December New Style, the Japanese blew up the parapet and captured the fort. The shattered casemates, ditch and caponiers remain visible. A stone erected by the Japanese marks the general’s death: “Place where Russian Major General Kondratenko fell.” A small museum stands nearby.
visit: Ctrip gives opening hours of 07:30–17:00. Admission is paid; travel agencies quote 25 yuan. Parking is at the entrance (东鸡冠山停车场). Check hours before travelling.

name: The Great Eagle’s Nest
name_zh: 望台炮台 (Wàngtái pàotái)
name_now: A height with a Japanese memorial marker and viewpoint beside Jiguan Shan Road
summary: A hilltop battery between Forts II and III on the northeastern front. Its fall on 19 December 1904 (1 January 1905 New Style) was the defence’s last major event: that same day Stessel sent the Japanese an offer to surrender. Old guns and a memorial marker now stand on the summit, with views along the hills from Jiguan Shan to Erlongshan. The identification of the Russian name with the Chinese Wangtai is generally accepted, but should be checked against the 1904 fortress plan.

name: Fort No. III
name_zh: 二龙山堡垒 (Èrlóngshān bǎolěi)
name_now: Fort ruins on Erlongshan
summary: A fort on the northern front, on Erlongshan west of the Great Eagle’s Nest. Japanese troops drove mine galleries towards it and captured it on 15 (28) December 1904 after blowing up the parapet. Parts of the ditch and concrete structures survive. The coordinates mark the hilltop; the fort itself lies on the slope, so its exact position needs checking on site.

name: Fortification No. 3
name_zh: 松树山堡垒 (Sōngshùshān bǎolěi)
name_now: Fortification ruins on Songshushan
summary: An intermediate work between the northern-front forts, built to the same basic scheme: rampart, dry ditch, caponiers and barracks. It fell on 18 (31) December 1904 after a Japanese mine beneath the parapet brought down a casemate. Ruins among pine trees and the explosion crater remain. It receives noticeably fewer visitors than 203 Metre Hill or Dongjiguanshan.

name: Fortification No. 5
name_zh: 鸦户嘴 (Yāhùzuǐ); signs call it the “Russian Army Command Fort”
name_now: A surviving fortification in woodland, with a museum room, fortress model and coastal gun
summary: An intermediate work on the western front between Forts V and VI. A published readiness memo reports Fortification No. 5 complete by 1 December 1903, while work on Fort VI had only just begun. According to the channel, Qing works preceded the Russian rebuilding after 1898; the precise sequence still needs verification. The channel reports no separate assault. The work was handed over at the capitulation, but had taken part in artillery action recorded in G. S. Pilsudski’s diary. Surviving features include rampart, dry ditch, caponiers, barracks and underground passages. The site displays a gun that the field report author identifies as a 10-inch coastal gun on a Durlacher mounting; its provenance is unestablished. A small museum room displays a fortress model and soldiers’ everyday life. The claim that 203 Metre Hill was commanded from here is not supported by documents.
visit: A quiet site that is not yet a regular tourist stop. The channel gives 38.7970, 121.1933 for navigation. Check access arrangements and whether a ticket is needed in advance.

name: Electric Cliff Battery
name_zh: 电岩炮台 (Diànyán pàotái)
name_now: A coastal battery memorial above the Yellow Sea
summary: Coastal Battery No. 15 stood on the cliff east of Gold Hill near the entrance to Port Arthur harbour. The name refers to a searchlight installed on the cliff. Within the first weeks of the war, the Russian press was already mentioning Electric Cliff in reports of the bombardment of the harbour. Traces of the battery survive on the cliff.
visit: One travel-agency account says foreigners cannot visit; other sources describe a normal paid attraction costing about 15 yuan. Check before travelling.

name: Golden Hill
name_zh: 黄金山 (Huángjīnshān)
name_now: Hill at the entrance to Lüshun harbour, partly within a military zone
summary: The eastern side of the harbour entrance, sheltering the inner basins from the sea together with Tiger’s Tail peninsula. Grand Duke Kirill Vladimirovich raised the Russian flag above Golden Hill on 16 (28) March 1898. Coastal batteries built under the Qing and rebuilt by the Russians stood here. Below it, on the outer roadstead, the squadron was attacked by Japanese destroyers on 27 January (9 February) 1904. A town beach is now at its foot; military installations occupy the summit.

name: Quail Hill (Baiyushan)
name_zh: 白玉山 (Báiyùshān)
name_now: Hilltop park with a Japanese tower from 1909 (白玉山塔), harbour views and a cable car
summary: The hill above the Eastern Basin between the Old and New Towns, from which panoramas of Russian Port Arthur were photographed. After the war, at Nogi and Tōgō’s initiative, the Japanese built the roughly 67 m Hyōchūtō, or “Loyalty Tower”, now 白玉山塔. The viewpoint overlooks the inner harbour, Golden Hill, Tiger’s Tail and the land-front hills, making it a useful place to begin a visit to Lüshun.
visit: A road and cable car (白玉山索道) reach the summit. Ticket reports differ: travel agencies variously quote 40 yuan admission or a free tower with a paid cable car. Check locally.

name: Port Arthur’s Inner Harbour (Eastern and Western Basins)
name_zh: 旅顺港 (Lǚshùn gǎng); 旅顺口 (Lǚshùnkǒu)
name_now: An active PLA Navy base, with a public waterfront and viewpoints beside the town
summary: Russia leased Kwantung for this harbour. Its narrow, deep entrance lies between Golden Hill and Tiger’s Tail, with two basins inside. The First Pacific Squadron was based here: seven battleships, cruisers and destroyers. After the loss of 203 Metre Hill, siege howitzers sank the ships beside the quays; only Sevastopol escaped, taken by Essen to White Wolf Bay. Today this is an active naval base. The civilian town reaches the water; the rest is viewed from Quail Hill. The coordinate is a representative point over the Eastern Basin.
visit: The base is closed to visitors. Photographing warships is not recommended.

name: Port Arthur Railway Station
name_zh: 旅顺站 (Lǚshùn zhàn)
name_now: A Russian-style wooden station on the waterfront; regular services have ended
summary: The Chinese Eastern Railway branch to the naval port of Port Arthur ended here. Liaoning’s heritage office dates the timber building to October 1900. A turret with fish-scale metal roofing marks the waiting room. In 1945 the station became part of the Chinese Changchun Railway, jointly run by China and the Soviet Union. It passed to Chinese administration in 1952. The metro station of the same name is farther north.
visit: 8 Jinggang Street (井岗街8号). The building can be seen from the street.

name: Port Arthur Prison
name_zh: 旅顺日俄监狱旧址 (Lǚshùn Rì-É jiānyù jiùzhǐ)
name_now: The Former Russo-Japanese Prison museum
summary: The Russians began building the prison in 1902; the Japanese enlarged it in 1907. Brickwork reveals the difference: the grey blocks by the entrance are Russian, the large red blocks Japanese. Under Japanese rule it held Chinese, Korean and Japanese prisoners. Korean independence activist An Jung-geun, who killed Itō Hirobumi, was executed here in 1910. The prison operated until 1945 and became a museum in 1971. Cells, workshops and the execution site survive.
visit: 139 Xiangyang Street (向阳街139号). The former prison is now a museum.

name: Port Arthur Russian and Soviet Military Cemetery
name_zh: 旅顺苏军烈士陵园 (Lǚshùn Sūjūn lièshì língyuán)
name_now: Soviet military memorial cemetery in Sanliqiao, with burials from 1904–1905 in the older section
summary: One of the largest Russian military cemeteries outside Russia. Founded during the Russian period, it was landscaped by the Japanese authorities after the war as a memorial to the fortress’s fallen defenders. The older section consists mainly of mass graves from 1904, with a chapel and monument. From 1945, Soviet servicemen who died in Port Arthur were buried here, followed by casualties of the Korean War. A 1955 Soviet military monument stands at the entrance. Russian specialists restored the cemetery in the 2000s. General Kondratenko is not buried here: his remains were taken to St Petersburg in 1905.

name: Lüshun Museum
name_zh: 旅顺博物馆 (Lǚshùn bówùguǎn)
name_now: A state museum in the New Town (Taiyanggou)
summary: Lüshun Museum grew out of an exhibition of products from Manchuria and Mongolia that the Japanese administration began organising in 1915. The museum opened to the public in April 1917. Its building combines European and East Asian forms. Its collections now include archaeological finds, bronzes, calligraphy and objects from Xinjiang.

name: Port Arthur’s New Town
name_zh: 太阳沟 (Tàiyánggōu)
name_now: The historic Taiyanggou district: quiet streets of Russian and Japanese villas
summary: The Russians laid out the New Town west of the harbour with straight, European-style streets; the channel mentions Morskaya and Pushkinskaya. Japanese administrative buildings followed. Russian villas, including one marked as a senior official’s residence (俄式高官住宅), now stand beside the former Kwantung Army headquarters, Lüshun Museum and the Soviet friendship tower. Trees line the streets, with black locust blossom in May.
visit: Allow 1–1.5 hours to walk the district’s streets from Lüshun Museum.

name: Sino-Soviet Friendship Tower
name_zh: 中苏友谊纪念塔 (Zhōng-Sū yǒuyì jìniàntǎ)
name_now: A monument on the square beside Lüshun Museum
summary: The Sino-Soviet Friendship Tower stands in front of Lüshun Museum. The foundation stone was laid in February 1955, construction was completed in October 1956 and the inauguration followed in February 1957. Reliefs around the base show Tiananmen and the Kremlin, the Anshan steelworks, views of Port Arthur and a harvest scene.
visit: The square is open; view the monument from outside.

name: The Meeting House at Shuishiying
name_zh: 水师营会见所旧址 (Shuǐshīyíng huìjiànsuǒ jiùzhǐ)
name_now: A memorial house on Lüshun’s northern outskirts
summary: In Shuishiying, north of Port Arthur, representatives of the two armies signed the surrender terms on 2 January 1905 (20 December 1904 Old Style). Three days later, on 5 January (23 December), Generals Nogi and Stessel met here. Japanese postcards document the meeting site. One shows the village house and a later memorial marker. Which parts of today’s building date to the early twentieth century remains unconfirmed.

name: Longwangtang: The Reservoir Cherry Garden
name_zh: 龙王塘樱花园 (Lóngwángtáng yīnghuā yuán)
name_now: A cherry-blossom park beside Longwangtang Reservoir (龙王塘水库)
summary: Longwangtang Cherry Blossom Park lies by the reservoir dam between Dalian and Lüshun. The garden and reservoir share one landscape: on the path near the pavilion you can see the flowering trees and the embankment. The cherries bloom in spring, with exact dates varying with the weather.
visit: Search for 龙王塘樱花园 on your map. Blossom dates vary by year.

name: Nikolayevskaya Square
name_zh: 中山广场 (Zhōngshān guǎngchǎng)
name_now: Zhongshan Square in central Dalian, a circular square surrounded by Japanese-era banks and a hotel
summary: The circle and its ten radiating streets took shape on the Russian plan of Dalny. Under Japanese administration it was called Ōhiroba, meaning Grand Square. Administrative buildings, banks and the Yamato Hotel went up around it from 1908. On 1 June 1946 it was named after Sun Yat-sen, also known in China as Sun Zhongshan. The Financial Building now occupies the former British consulate site.
visit: Metro: Zhongshan Square station (中山广场站). The square is open around the clock; buildings are illuminated in the evening.

name: Russian Street (Formerly Inzhenernaya)
name_zh: 团结街 / 俄罗斯风情街 (Tuánjié jiē / Éluósī fēngqíng jiē)
name_now: A pedestrian tourist street in the former Russian administrative quarter
summary: A street in Dalny’s earliest district, north of the railway, where the administrative quarter was built in 1899–1902. The channel identifies former Inzhenernaya Street with today’s Russian Street. Some houses are original; much was added or restored in an “old-fashioned” style when the street became a tourist attraction. Souvenir shops occupy ground floors. Dalny’s city administration building stands at the far end.
visit: A 15–20 minute walk from Zhongshan Square across Victory Bridge. The street is always open.

name: Dalny City Administration Building
name_zh: 达里尼市政厅旧址 (Dálǐní shìzhèngtīng jiùzhǐ)
name_now: A historic building at the northern end of Russian Street
summary: One of Dalny’s first masonry buildings, erected for the city administration in the early 1900s. Vladimir Sakharov, engineer, port builder and first city governor, administered Dalny from here. He volunteered for Port Arthur in 1904 and died there of typhus. Japanese institutions occupied the building after 1905; it later housed Dalian’s Natural History Museum for many years. It is now a protected monument, though the museum inside may be closed.

name: The 1902 Building by the Bridge (Chinese Eastern Railway Office)
name_zh: 大连艺术展览馆 / 大连美术馆 (Dàlián yìshù zhǎnlǎnguǎn / Dàlián měishùguǎn)
name_now: Dalian Art Museum
summary: The turreted building at the entrance to Russian Street is known as the former East China Steamship Company office. Liaoning’s heritage office dates the start of construction to 1902, credits the design to Kazimierz Skolimowski and records its use by the Russian administration and later a Japanese steamship company. The building was reconstructed for art exhibitions in 1998. In 2001 the site received national heritage protection.

name: Victory Bridge
name_zh: 胜利桥 (Shènglì qiáo)
name_now: A bridge over the railway between Russian Street and the city centre
summary: A bridge linking the Russian administrative quarter with the rest of Dalny across the railway tracks. Called Nipponbashi under Japanese rule, it became Victory Bridge after 1945. It offers views of the buildings north of the tracks. Sources disagree on the first bridge’s construction and later rebuilding; a Japanese reconstruction in the late 1900s is often mentioned.
visit: The bridge links central Dalian with Russian Street and carries a pavement.

name: Western Park (City Garden?)
name_zh: 劳动公园 (Láodòng gōngyuán)
name_now: Labour Park, the largest park in central Dalian
summary: According to Chinese sources, the Russians founded the park in 1898 on what was then the western edge of town and called it Western Park. The Japanese expanded it with sumo, golf and a swimming pool, renaming it Central Park in 1926. It became Lenin Park in 1947 and Labour Park in 1949. The channel has a photograph captioned “City Garden” in Dalny, but whether it shows this park has not been established. Ginkgo trees turn yellow here in autumn.
visit: Admission is free. The east entrance (劳动公园东门) is a 10–15 minute walk from Zhongshan Square.

name: Dalny Port (Victoria Bay)
name_zh: 大连港 (Dàlián gǎng)
name_now: Dalian Port, with its passenger terminal (大连港客运站) and Gangwan Square
summary: The city was built for this port, designed by Vladimir Sakharov, who had previously built Vladivostok’s commercial harbour. The first phase cost 10.8 million rubles and immediately made Dalny China’s second-busiest cargo port after Shanghai. In May 1904, Japanese troops captured the nearly completed port and used it to supply the army besieging Port Arthur. It remains a major working port; its passenger terminal faces the city. The coordinate marks the terminal.
visit: The passenger terminal is open to ferry passengers; the cargo port is closed.

name: Yamato Hotel
name_zh: 大连宾馆 (Dàlián bīnguǎn), formerly 大和旅馆
name_now: Former Dalian Hotel, 4 Zhongshan Square
summary: The Yamato Hotel building on the south side of Zhongshan Square was completed in 1914. The hotel had been receiving guests at another address since 1907. It was run by the South Manchuria Railway, which had a chain of hotels in cities along its line. The building later became the Dalian Hotel. Accor lists the property as the forthcoming Fairmont Dalian.
visit: 4 Zhongshan Square. The columned façade can be seen from the square.

name: Yokohama Specie Bank Branch
name_zh: 横滨正金银行大连支店旧址 (Héngbīn Zhèngjīn yínháng), now 中国银行
name_now: A Bank of China branch
summary: A three-domed building from 1909, designed by Tsumaki Yorinaka, a leading Meiji-era Japanese architect, and his pupil Ōta Satoshi. The Yokohama Specie Bank financed foreign trade; Manchurian soybeans and soybean cake passed through Dairen. A Bank of China branch now occupies the building, with a 2005 extension behind it.
visit: A working bank.

name: Dairen City Hall
name_zh: 大连市役所旧址 (Dàlián shìyìsuǒ), now 中国工商银行
name_now: An ICBC branch
summary: The former Dairen City Hall occupies No. 5 Zhongshan Square. In 1922 the Japanese civil administration moved here from No. 2. Its projecting entrance and tower stand out among the buildings facing the circle. The Industrial and Commercial Bank of China later used the premises.
visit: A working bank.

name: Dairen Police Headquarters
name_zh: 大连警察署旧址 (Dàlián jǐngchá shǔ)
name_now: Former Dairen Civil Administration Office, 2 Zhongshan Square
summary: The red-brick building on today’s Zhongshan Square was built in 1908 for the Japanese civil administration of Dairen, to a design by the architect Maeda (前田松韻). In 1922 the administration moved into the city hall on the same square and the police took over the premises. Both names appear in guidebooks.
visit: 2 Zhongshan Square. The façade is visible from the outer pavement.

name: Dairen Railway Station
name_zh: 大连站 (Dàlián zhàn)
name_now: Dalian’s main railway station
summary: Opened in 1937, the station separated passenger flows by level: departing passengers ascended ramps to the upper floor, while arrivals left below. Its exterior is often compared with Tokyo’s Ueno Station. Built by the Japanese for the expanding city, it is a different building from Russian Dalny’s station. It remains in use, with a large forecourt.
visit: An operating station. Metro: Dalian Railway Station.

name: Russian Cemetery at Goshinji Temple, Nagasaki
name_zh: 悟真寺国際墓地 (Japanese: Goshinji kokusai bochi; Chinese: Wùzhēnsì)
name_now: Inasa International Cemetery at the Buddhist Goshinji Temple
summary: The Russian Pacific Squadron wintered in Nagasaki until 1897, and a Russian sailors’ cemetery grew up at Goshinji Temple in Inasa. The infant Mikhail Mühlberg lies here: born in besieged Port Arthur on 13 November 1904, baptised the day after the surrender, he lived 52 days. Historian Dmitry Nikolayev reconstructed his family’s story from parish registers in “Misha from Nagasaki”, published in Rodina.
visit: The temple is in Inasa on the western shore of Nagasaki Bay, near Goshinji-mae bus stop (悟真寺前).

name: Dalian University of Foreign Languages, Lüshun Campus
name_zh: 大连外国语大学（旅顺校区）
name_now: A working university; Russian Club of Dalian excursions meet outside the campus gates
summary: Meeting point for the Russian Club of Dalian’s guided Port Arthur excursions, usually around 09:00, with a return transfer here. The campus stands in the new university district east of Lüshun, about 5 km in a straight line from the historic centre and station. The campus itself has no connection with the fortress: it is a convenient meeting point with parking and an address taxis can find. The group continues by car, beginning at Port Arthur station.
visit: The organisers will specify the exact meeting point at the campus gates and the time; confirm the day before. Search for 大连外国语大学 旅顺校区.

name: Port Arthur’s Old Town
name_zh: 旅顺老城区（黄河路一带）
name_now: Central Lüshun east of Quail Hill, with Russian and Japanese houses beside the Eastern Basin
summary: The town beside the Eastern Basin, below Golden and Quail hills, grew up in the days of the Qing fleet. During Russian rule, Pacific Squadron officers and sailors lived here among port offices, shops and restaurants, while the New Town on the western shore was still being built. The Japanese remodelled the centre after 1905, and many buildings visible today are Japanese-era. The map point represents the district, which is best explored on foot.
visit: Walk from the railway station or the lower Quail Hill cable-car station. Do not photograph military installations beside the harbour. Check locally which buildings are open.

name: Redoubt No. 1 (East Panlongshan)
name_zh: 盘龙山东堡垒 (Pánlóngshān dōng bǎolěi)
name_now: Remains of a fieldwork in front of the fort line, north of the Great Eagle’s Nest
summary: Russian accounts identify Eastern Panlongshan Redoubt as No. 1. It stood in front of Port Arthur’s main defensive line beside Western Redoubt No. 2. Japanese troops captured both redoubts during the first general assault in August 1904. A Japanese photograph taken after the capture shows the gorge at the rear of the redoubt. The exact location of surviving remains still needs field verification.
visit: There is no separate visitor area. The approximate point comes from the 1904 fortress plan. Look for earthwork remains north of Jiguan Shan Road.

name: Redoubt No. 2 (West Panlongshan)
name_zh: 盘龙山西堡垒 (Pánlóngshān xī bǎolěi)
name_now: Remains of a fieldwork in front of the fort line, east of Erlongshan
summary: Russian accounts identify Western Panlongshan Redoubt as No. 2. Together with the eastern redoubt, it covered the approaches to Port Arthur’s main defensive line. Both redoubts fell in August 1904. A Japanese photograph taken after the capture shows a shelter in the western redoubt. The exact location of surviving remains still needs field verification.
visit: The approximate position comes from the 1904 plan. Any signs are in Chinese only.

name: Fortification No. 4
name_zh: 大案子山堡垒 (Dà Ànzishān bǎolěi)
name_now: A fortification on Great Anzishan north of the New Town, marked as a viewpoint on OpenStreetMap
summary: The fortification on Da’anzishan stood on the western front of Port Arthur, between Forts IV and V. On the map from the end of the siege it was still within the Russian lines. It passed to the Japanese after the fortress surrendered. The project’s photographs show the stone wall of the dry ditch, arched openings and remnants of the concrete parapet.
visit: Approach from the New Town streets (民泰街). Check access and ticket arrangements in advance.

name: Fort No. IV
name_zh: 椅子山堡垒 (Yǐzishān bǎolěi)
name_now: A fort on Yizishan northwest of the New Town
summary: A Western Front fort on Yizishan, or “Chair Hill”, on the northern flank and closest to 203 Metre Hill among this sector’s forts. On the 1904 plan, it remains Russian until the siege ends, like all the western forts: after taking 203 Metre Hill on 22 November (5 December), the Japanese did not advance farther west. The fortress surrendered on 20 December 1904 (2 January 1905), and the fort was occupied without fighting. The OpenStreetMap position agrees with the 1904 plan.
visit: Approach along Chuncheng Road (春城路). We have no ticket information; check locally.

name: Battery D
name_now: Site of a permanent battery between Fort No. V and Fortification No. 5
summary: Port Arthur’s land-front batteries were designated by letters. On the Military Historical Commission’s plan showing the defences on 19 December 1904 Old Style, the mark “Бат. Д” is south of Fort No. V. G. S. Piłsudski wrote about the battery’s role in the artillery fighting that December. Its exact position on modern maps and any surviving remains need verification. No photograph of the battery has been confirmed.

name: Naval Assembly
name_now: Building not yet identified; the map point is provisional
summary: The Naval Assembly was the naval officers’ club in Russian Port Arthur. A Russian postcard shows a gate with a circular opening and decorative latticework. The same gate can be recognised in a Japanese album published in 1922, where it is captioned as the Suikōsha naval club (水交社). The exact modern address and the subsequent fate of the compound remain unknown. The map pin indicates the tour stop in the New Town.
visit: Shown on the guided excursion. For independent visits, follow the guide’s description. The map position is provisional.

name: Yamato Hotel, Lüshun
name_zh: 旅顺大和旅馆旧址 (Lǚshùn Dàhé lǚguǎn jiùzhǐ), 文化路30号
name_now: A two-storey mansion of 1903 on Wenhua Road, reported by the press to be in poor condition
summary: Distinguish it from Dalian’s Yamato Hotel on Zhongshan Square. The protected-building plaque dates it to 1903. Chinese press reports identify it as the mansion of Ji Fengtai, a Chinese merchant with Russian nationality, converted after the war into a South Manchuria Railway Yamato hotel. The same reports say Puyi stayed here in 1931. In the late 2010s, journalists described cracks in the walls and a construction fence around the house.
visit: Address: 旅顺口区文化路30号, west of Lüshun Museum. The map point marks the street rather than the house; access inside is unlikely.

name: Russian School
name_now: Building not yet identified; the map point in the New Town is provisional
summary: Port Arthur had several Russian schools, among them the Pushkin School, whose building appears on a postcard published by Fortuna. Which school corresponds to the tour stop called “Russian School” in the New Town remains uncertain. The map pin identifies the general area.
visit: Shown on the guided excursion. The map position is provisional.

name: Lüshun’s Japanese Quarters
name_zh: 太阳沟历史街区 (中央大街、新华大街一带)
name_now: Taiyanggou streets with administrative buildings and villas from 1905–1945
summary: After 1905, the Japanese made Lüshun, or Ryojun, the capital of Kwantung and developed the New Town begun by the Russians. Buildings include the former Kwantung administration, gendarmerie headquarters, the mansion of Manchu Prince Su, who lived here after the Qing fell, schools and Japanese officials’ houses. Many have protected-monument plaques; some are abandoned. The point represents the district, easily explored on foot from the museum.
visit: Allow 1–1.5 hours to walk from Lüshun Museum along Zhongyang Avenue and Xinhua Avenue. Building plaques are in Chinese.

name: Red Cross Hospital
name_zh: 旅顺红十字医院旧址 (Lǚshùn Hóngshízì yīyuàn jiùzhǐ)
name_now: Former Red Cross Hospital, 107 Huanghe Road
summary: Construction began in 1900 on the Huanghe Road building for Port Arthur’s municipal hospital. The Liaoning heritage register lists 40 wards. The Japanese Red Cross Society took it over in March 1905. In 1907 it became the society’s hospital for the Kwantung Leased Territory. The complex passed to Soviet administration in 1945 and has been used by the Chinese navy since 1955.
visit: 107 Huanghe Road (黄河路107号). The provincial register includes historical and modern photographs of the building.

name: General Kondratenko’s House
name_zh: 康特拉琴柯旧居 (Kāngtèlāqínkē jiùjū)
name_now: A 1903 residence on Ningbo Street
summary: Major General Roman Kondratenko, who commanded the land defences of Port Arthur, lived in the house on what is now Ningbo Street. The Liaoning register identifies the building, which dates to 1903, as his former residence. He was killed at Fort No. II on 15 December 1904 (2 December Old Style). His remains were taken to St Petersburg in 1905.
visit: 47 Ningbo Street (宁波街47号), New Town. The façade can be seen from the street.

name: Laotieshan Lighthouse
name_zh: 老铁山灯塔 (Lǎotiěshān dēngtǎ)
name_now: An operating lighthouse and viewpoint at the southern tip of the Liaodong peninsula
summary: The lighthouse marks the southern end of the Liaodong Peninsula, near the conventional boundary between the Yellow and Bohai Seas. The Qing maritime customs service built the iron tower in 1893. It housed a French-made mechanism in which the optics rotated on a mercury bearing. The light guided ships around the cape as they sailed to Port Arthur or into the Bohai Gulf.
visit: About 20 km from central Lüshun, by car or taxi. Travel agencies report paid admission to the viewing area; check hours. The cape is very windy.

name: Great Black Mountain (Dahei Shan)
name_zh: 大黑山 (Dàhēishān)
name_now: The highest mountain in Dalian’s six districts, 663 m
summary: A 663 m mountain in Jinzhou district, part of the Qianshan range, with Dalian University’s campus at its foot. It has no direct connection with Port Arthur or Dalny: it is a place for a countryside walk. Rhododendrons and other flowers bloom on the slopes and near the summit in spring.

name: Xinghai Square
name_zh: 星海广场 (Xīnghǎi Guǎngchǎng)
name_now: Waterfront square in Shahekou District
summary: Dalian’s Xinghai Square stands on land that was part of the bay in the early 1990s. The city began reclaiming the coastal shallows in 1993. Construction of the square was completed on 30 June 1997 for Hong Kong’s return to China. Two years later, a sculpture commemorating the centenary of Dalian was installed by the seafront. A walkway lined with residents’ footprints leads to a sculpture in the shape of an open book. Follow the footprints towards the water and the suspension span of the bay bridge comes into view behind the book.
visit: From Xinghai Square station on metro line 1, walk towards the open circle of the square, then south towards the sea.

name: Xinghai Bay Bridge
name_zh: 星海湾跨海大桥 (Xīnghǎiwān Kuàhǎi Dàqiáo)
name_now: Double-deck road bridge in southern Dalian
summary: When Xinghai Bay Bridge opened on 30 October 2015, Dalian gained a coastal road that bypassed the congested Zhongshan West Road (中山西路). The bridge route runs for 6.8 km, including an 820 m suspension section. The road runs on two levels. Massive offshore anchor blocks secure the main cables. The suspension section stands about a kilometre offshore, aligned with the centreline of Xinghai Square so it can be seen from the square.
visit: For a view of the two towers and the suspension span, walk to the waterfront at the southern end of Xinghai Square. The map pin marks the bridge out in the bay.
